children.name: Aptenodytes
children.description: The great penguins — the largest and most iconic penguin species, comprising the Emperor and King Penguins. Aptenodytes species are distinguished by their large size, vivid orange-yellow ear patches, and a unique breeding biology: Kings incubate eggs on their feet over winter, while Emperors breed on Antarctic sea ice in the dead of winter, enduring temperatures below -60°C.

children.name: Aptenodytes forsteri
children.description: The emperor penguin (Aptenodytes forsteri) is the tallest and heaviest of all living penguin species and lives exclusively in Antarctica.

children.name: Aptenodytes patagonicus
children.description: The king penguin (Aptenodytes patagonicus) is the second largest species of penguin, smaller than but somewhat similar in appearance to the emperor penguin.

children.name: Pygoscelis
children.description: Brush-tailed penguins — medium-sized Antarctic penguins named for their long, stiff tail feathers that brush the ground when walking. They are the most abundant penguins on Earth, with Adélie and Chinstrap colonies numbering in the millions. All three species breed on the Antarctic continent and subantarctic islands.

children.name: Pygoscelis adeliae
children.description: The Adélie penguin (Pygoscelis adeliae) is a species of penguin common along the entire coast of the Antarctic continent. It is the most widespread penguin species in the Antarctic, and, along with the emperor penguin, is the most southerly distributed of all penguins. It is named after Adélie Land, in turn, named for Adèle Dumont d'Urville, who was married to French explorer Jules Dumont d'Urville, who first discovered this penguin in 1840. Adélie penguins obtain their food by both predation and foraging, with a diet of mainly krill and fish.

children.name: Pygoscelis antarcticus
children.description: The chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarcticus) is a penguin species that inhabits various islands and shores in the Southern Pacific and the Antarctic Oceans.

children.name: Pygoscelis papua
children.description: The gentoo penguin ( ) (Pygoscelis papua) is a penguin species (or possibly a species complex) in the genus Pygoscelis, most closely related to the Adélie penguin (P.

children.name: Eudyptes
children.description: The crested penguins — medium-sized penguins with prominent yellow or orange feather crests above the eyes. Found on subantarctic and temperate islands of the Southern Ocean. Most species have a distinctive 'bouncing' walk and a harsh, braying call. Several species are among the most threatened penguins, with populations declining sharply due to climate change and overfishing.

children.name: Eudyptes chrysolophus
children.description: The macaroni penguin (Eudyptes chrysolophus) is a species of penguin found from the Subantarctic to the Antarctic Peninsula.

children.name: Eudyptes chrysocome
children.description: The western rockhopper penguin (Eudyptes chrysocome) is a species of rockhopper penguin.

children.name: Eudyptes schlegeli
children.description: The royal penguin (Eudyptes schlegeli) is a species of penguin, which can be found only on the sub-Antarctic Macquarie Island and adjacent islands.

children.name: Eudyptes filholi
children.description: The eastern rockhopper penguin (Eudyptes filholi), also known as the tawaki kaipiki toka, is a crested penguin with yellow crest feathers. It was formerly treated as conspecific with the western rockhopper penguin with the name "southern rockhopper penguin" for the combined species. It is one of the smallest crested penguins and has distinctive pink margins around its bill. It breeds on islands in the Southern Indian and Pacific Oceans.

children.name: Eudyptes pachyrhynchus
children.description: The Fiordland penguin (Eudyptes pachyrhynchus), also known as the Fiordland crested penguin (in Māori, tawaki or pokotiwha), is a crested penguin species endemic to New Zealand.

children.name: Eudyptes sclateri
children.description: The erect-crested penguin (Eudyptes sclateri;) is a penguin endemic to the New Zealand region and only breeds on the Bounty and Antipodes Islands. It has black upper parts, white underparts and a yellow eye stripe and crest. It spends the winter at sea and little is known about its biology and breeding habits. Populations are believed to have declined during the last few decades of the twentieth century, and the International Union for Conservation of Nature has listed it as being "endangered".

children.name: Megadyptes
children.description: The yellow-eyed penguin — a monotypic genus endemic to New Zealand. Distinguished by its pale yellow eyes and yellow head band. Considered the rarest penguin species, with around 4,000 individuals remaining. It is the only penguin with a solitary, non-colonial breeding style, nesting in coastal scrub and forest.

children.name: Megadyptes antipodes
children.description:
The yellow-eyed penguin (Megadyptes antipodes), known also as hoiho, is a species of penguin endemic to New Zealand. It is the sole extant species in the genus Megadyptes, from Ancient Greek μέγας, meaning "large", and δύπτης, meaning "diver".
Previously thought closely related to the little penguin (Eudyptula minor), molecular research has shown it more closely related to penguins of the genus Eudyptes. Like most penguins, it is mainly piscivorous.

children.name: Megadyptes waitaha
children.authorship: Boessenkool, Austin, Worthy, Scofield, Cooper, Seddon & Waters, 2009

children.name: Eudyptula
children.description: The little penguins — the smallest penguins in the world, found only in Australia and New Zealand. Nocturnal on land to avoid predators, they return to their burrows after dark in 'penguin parades' that have become major tourist attractions. Their slate-blue plumage gives them the alternative name 'fairy penguins'.

children.name: Eudyptula minor
children.description: The little penguin (Eudyptula minor) is the smallest species of penguin in the world, and originates from New Zealand and Australia.

children.name: Eudyptula albosignata
children.description: The little penguin (Eudyptula minor) is the smallest species of penguin in the world, and originates from New Zealand and Australia.

children.name: Spheniscus
children.description: The banded penguins — medium-sized penguins of temperate and tropical coasts, distinguished by a characteristic black band across the chest. Unlike Antarctic penguins, they inhabit warmer waters and have bare facial patches that help dissipate heat. The genus includes the only penguin species found north of the Equator (Galápagos Penguin).

children.name: Spheniscus demersus
children.description: The African penguin (Spheniscus demersus), also known as Cape penguin or South African penguin, is a species of penguin confined to southern African waters.

children.name: Spheniscus magellanicus
children.description: The Magellanic penguin (Spheniscus magellanicus) is a South American penguin, breeding in coastal Patagonia, including Argentina, Chile, and the Falkland Islands, with some migrating to Brazil and Uruguay, where they are occasionally seen as far north as Espírito Santo.

children.name: Spheniscus mendiculus
children.description: The Galápagos penguin (Spheniscus mendiculus) is a penguin endemic to the Galápagos Islands of Ecuador.
